rows.question: Will the first commercially successful personal robot use legs?
rows.scored_text:
Will the first commercially successful personal robot use legs?
This market closes on December 4, 2031.
Resolution rules: Defined as the first robot designed to have general capability with household tasks (so it can't just be like a roomba). First model to sell over 1 million units to consumers. Will it walk with legs? Resolution criteria This market resolves YES if the first general-purpose personal household robot model to sell more than 1,000,000 units to consumers uses legs (bipedal, quadrupedal, or other legged locomotion) as its primary means of movement. This market resolves NO if the first such robot to reach this milestone relies primarily on wheels, tracks, a fixed/stationary base, or another non-legged mechanism for movement. Key definitions & edge cases: General capability / household robot: The model must be designed and marketed for general-purpose domestic manipulation or multi-task assistance (e.g., tidying, handling objects, folding laundry, kitchen prep). Single-purpose appliances such as robotic vacuum cleaners (e.g., Roomba), robotic lawnmowers, or pool cleaners do not qualify. Sales threshold: The robot model (or a single continuous product family/hardware generation) must surpass 1,000,000 cumulative units delivered or sold directly to retail consumers, verified by official manufacturer financial disclosures, audited company press releases, or consensus reporting from credible business/tech outlets (e.g., Bloomberg, Reuters, The Wall Street Journal). Enterprise/industrial-only sales do not count toward the consumer threshold. Locomotion: "Using legs" requires articulated mechanical limbs for ambulatory locomotion. Hybrid systems (e.g., wheels mounted on the ends of legs) resolve based on the primary, default locomotion method specified by the manufacturer; if both legs and wheels are integral to standard operation, the creator may evaluate whether ambulatory stepping is essential to the design or edit the criteria if clarification is needed. Background The consumer robotics industry is divided on locomotion for home environments: Legged / Humanoid: Proponents (e.g., Tesla with Optimus, Figure, Unitree, Boston Dynamics) argue that human environments (stairs, narrow doorways, multi-level homes) are fundamentally designed for bipedal or legged navigation, making legs necessary for true general utility. Wheeled / Mobile Base: Competitors and roboticists often point to wheels or continuous tracks as significantly cheaper, more power-efficient, and safer around household occupants, avoiding the complex balance and high actuator costs associated with dynamic walking. Will a moving mirror produce light that propagates below c in vacuum by the end of 2030?
This market closes on December 31, 2030.
Resolution rules: I propose an experiment to test whether reflection from a moving surface changes light’s propagation speed in vacuum. A laser reflects from the rim of a rotating disk, with the reflected beam travelling approximately opposite to the local direction of the rim’s motion , towards a detector. The reflecting surface is therefore moving away from the detector. My model, Matter as Machine, predicts an outgoing speed of approximately c − 2v , where v is the rim’s local speed, under the simplified assumptions described in the proposal. The experiment would compare reference pulses with reflected pulses at different rotation speeds and propagation distances. This would help distinguish a propagation-speed change from changes in optical path length or apparatus timing. Read the proposed experiment and prediction:( https://matterasmachine.com/articles/predictions/slow-photons ). If confirmed and demonstrated to be incompatible with special relativity, this effect would constitute evidence against the theory. Such a discovery could be Nobel Prize-worthy, potentially bringing recognition to those who carry out and establish the result. Neither the outcome nor a prize is guaranteed. Resolution criteria Resolves YES if, by 31 December 2030, 23:59 UTC , publicly available results from this experiment or an equivalent moving-reflector experiment demonstrate: - An outgoing propagation speed below c in vacuum that depends on the reflector’s motion. - An additional delay that increases with post-reflection propagation distance, after accounting for optical path-length changes. - Independent replication, with reported uncertainties sufficient to distinguish the effect from measurement error. A delay attributable solely to known spatial-structure effects, optical components, detector response or changing path length does not qualify. The result need not match c − 2v exactly. This market concerns the existence of the specified slowdown, not confirmation of the entire Matter as Machine model. Resolves NO otherwise, including if no qualifying experiment is completed or the results remain inconclusive by the deadline. Disclosure I developed Matter as Machine and proposed the linked experiment. The prediction has not been experimentally confirmed.
